title: Vocab in Context — Core Skills
summary:
# Vocab in Context: The Basics

Some SAT questions pull a word out of a short paragraph and leave a blank. Here is the good news: you do not have to already know the word. The paragraph tells you what belongs there.

Every one of these paragraphs contains a clue — the part that explains or describes the blank. It usually sits right after a colon or semicolon, or in the sentence next door. Read the clue, then say the answer in your own everyday words. Then find the choice that means about the same thing.

One shortcut helps a lot: before you look at the choices, decide whether the blank needs a good word or a bad word. Just a plus or a minus in your head. That alone rules out about half the options most of the time.

Also watch the little signal words. But, however, although, and yet mean the next part turns the opposite direction. Because, since, and for example mean the next part goes the same direction and usually explains.

title: Central Ideas & Details — Core Skills
summary:
# Central Ideas: The Basics

Two question types show up over and over on the reading section. A central idea question asks what the whole paragraph is about. A detail question asks what the passage says about one specific thing. They sound alike, but they want opposite-sized answers, so read the question first.

Think of a central idea as a roof. It has to sit over every sentence in the passage, not just one. The most common wrong answer is a statement that is true but too small — it covers a single line. If a choice matches only one sentence, it is a detail, not the central idea.

Detail questions are easier than they look. The answer is written in the passage. You are locating a line, not deciding anything. Wrong choices there are usually true in real life but never appear in the text.

In short passages, the main point often lands in the first or last sentence. And always answer from the page: if the passage disagrees with what you already know, the passage wins.

title: Command of Evidence — Core Skills
summary:
# Command of Evidence: The Basics

Evidence is proof. It is the fact, number, quote, or example that backs up a claim. A claim is something someone says is true; evidence is what makes you believe it.

The SAT asks one question in many outfits: which choice best supports the claim? Good evidence does two things. First, it is about the same thing as the claim — that is what relevant means. If the claim is about cost, a fact about color does nothing, no matter how interesting. Second, it actually settles the point instead of landing somewhere nearby.

A useful habit: underline the claim, then finish this sentence before reading the choices — "To believe this, I would need to see ______." Then cross out any choice that is about the wrong subject.

Some evidence is stronger than other evidence. Measured data, study results, and direct quotes from the text are strong. One person's story or an emotional appeal with no facts behind it is weak. And if a graph appears, read the title, axis labels, and units before the bars.

title: Reading Comprehension — Core Skills
summary:
# Reading Comprehension: The Basics

Every reading passage on the SAT is short, usually five sentences or fewer. That is a real advantage, because you can read the whole thing. Three question types cover most of what you will see.

Main idea asks what the passage is mostly about. The right answer covers every sentence; a choice that matches only one line is too small.

Structure asks how the passage is put together, not what its facts are. Look for the turn word. "It is widely believed... but" means the passage sets up a belief and then knocks it down. "For example" means a claim followed by support. "Unlike" or "by contrast" means two things are being compared.

Support asks which fact would back up a claim. Find the claim, then pick the choice on the same subject that actually settles it.

Watch for choices that go further than the passage does. Words like all, never, and proves are worth a second look. And always answer from the page, not from what you already know.

title: Punctuation — Core Skills
summary:
# Punctuation: The Basics

SAT punctuation questions really ask one thing: where does one sentence stop and the next one start?

A **clause** is a group of words with a subject and a verb. A clause that can stand alone is **independent**. "The bus was late" is independent.

Two independent clauses cannot be joined by a comma alone. That mistake is a **comma splice**. Fix it three ways: a period, a semicolon, or a comma plus a FANBOYS word (for, and, nor, but, or, yet, so).

Three more patterns show up often. Put a comma after an opening phrase: *Before the game, we ate pizza.* Put a complete sentence before any colon: *I packed three things: a hat, a map, and water.* When extra information sits in the middle, use the same mark on both sides: *My uncle, who lives in Texas, sends postcards.*

title: Sentence Structure — Core Skills
summary:
# Sentence Structure: The Basics

Every sentence-structure question comes down to one check: is this a complete sentence?

A **clause** has a subject and a verb. An **independent clause** can stand alone: "The students packed up." A **dependent clause** cannot, because of the word it starts with — because, although, since, when, while, if. "When the bell rang" leaves you waiting.

A **fragment** is a piece punctuated like a sentence that is not one. Fix it by attaching it to a complete sentence: *When the bell rang, the students packed up.* When the dependent clause comes first, put a comma after it.

A **run-on** is the opposite problem: two complete sentences pushed together without the right punctuation. Fix it with a period, a semicolon, or a comma plus a FANBOYS word (for, and, nor, but, or, yet, so).

title: Transitions & Organization — Core Skills
summary:
# Transitions: The Basics

A **transition** is a word or short phrase that connects two sentences. On the SAT you get two sentences with a blank between them, and you pick the word that names how they are related.

There are six families to know. **Adding**: also, in addition, furthermore. **Contrast**: however, but, on the other hand, nevertheless. **Cause and effect**: therefore, so, as a result. **Example**: for example, for instance, specifically. **Sequence**: first, next, then, finally. **Conclusion**: in conclusion, ultimately, in short.

The method that works every time: cover the blank and the choices. Say the sentence before it in your own words, then the sentence after it. Ask one question — same direction, or opposite? Opposite means contrast. Only then look at the choices.

Organization questions ask where a sentence belongs. Follow the pointing-back words — she, it, this, they. Whatever they point to must already have been named.

title: Word Choice — Core Skills
summary:
# Word Choice: The Basics

Some SAT questions give you four choices that all mean about the same thing. Nothing is misspelled. The question asks which choice says it **most concisely** — the same meaning in the fewest words.

The answer is the shortest choice that still keeps every piece of the meaning. Compare *Due to the fact that the wind was strong, the race ended up being canceled* with *The race was canceled because the wind was too strong.* Both give the same two facts, and the second uses fewer words.

Watch for phrases that say the same thing twice: free gift, combined together, past history, in the year 1937. Watch for verbs stretched into phrases: *made a decision* is just *decided*.

Other questions show a student's notes and a goal. The right answer covers every part of the goal. A choice can be perfectly true and still be wrong if it only covers half.

title: Linear Equations & Inequalities — Core Skills
summary:
# Linear Equations: The Basics

An equation is two things that are equal, with an equals sign between them. A variable is a letter that stands for a number you do not know yet, and it is usually $x$. Solving means getting $x$ alone on one side so you can read the answer.

There is one rule: whatever you do to one side, do the same thing to the other side. To get $x$ alone, undo what is being done to it. Undo adding by subtracting, and undo multiplying by dividing. Handle adding and subtracting first, then multiplying and dividing.

Inequalities use the signs greater than, less than, or the versions with a line underneath. You solve them the same way. The only extra rule is this: if you multiply or divide both sides by a negative number, flip the direction of the sign.

Always put your answer back into the original problem to check it.

title: Systems of Equations — Core Skills
summary:
# Systems of Equations: The Basics

A system is two equations that are true at the same time. They share the same $x$ and the same $y$. The solution is the one pair of numbers that makes both equations true, and it is written as a point, $(x, y)$.

There are two methods you need. The first is substitution. Use it when one equation already tells you what a variable equals, like $y = 4$ or $y = 3x$. Put that value into the other equation in place of the variable, then solve for the letter that is left.

The second method is adding the equations. Use it when one equation has a plus $y$ and the other has a minus $y$. Stack them and add straight down. The $y$ terms cancel, leaving one easy equation.

Once you know one variable, put it back into either equation to find the other.

title: Graphing Inequalities — Core Skills
summary:
# Graphing Inequalities: The Basics

An equation like $y = 2x + 1$ draws a line. An inequality like $y > 2x + 1$ draws a whole region, which is a shaded area on one side of that line.

Every graph like this has exactly two decisions. The first is the line type. The line itself is called the boundary line. If the sign has a small line underneath it, meaning greater than or equal to, or less than or equal to, then points on the line count and you draw a solid line. If the sign has no line underneath, points on the line do not count and you draw a dashed line.

The second decision is the shading. Get $y$ alone on the left. Greater than means shade above the line. Less than means shade below it.

When you are unsure, test the point $(0, 0)$ and see if it makes the inequality true.

title: Ratios & Percents — Core Skills
summary:
# Ratios and Percents: The Basics

A ratio compares two amounts. If a bag has 6 red marbles and 9 blue marbles, the ratio of red to blue is 6 to 9. You simplify a ratio the way you simplify a fraction, by dividing both numbers by the same value, so 6 to 9 becomes 2 to 3.

A proportion says two ratios are equal. To solve one, look at how the bottom numbers are related, then do the same thing to the top numbers. Keep the same kind of amount on top on both sides.

Percent means out of one hundred. To find a percent of a number, turn the percent into a decimal by moving the decimal point two places left, then multiply, because the word of means multiply.

For a discount, find the amount that comes off first, then subtract it from the original price.

title: Functions — Core Skills
summary:
# Functions: The Basics

A function is a rule. You put a number in, the rule does something to it, and one number comes out. Think of a vending machine: press the same button and you always get the same snack.

The name $f(x)$ is read f of x. The letter $f$ is the name of the function, $x$ is the number you put in, and $f(x)$ is the number that comes out. It does not mean $f$ times $x$.

To evaluate a function, wherever you see $x$, write the input number instead, then do the arithmetic. Multiply before you add.

Many SAT functions look like $f(x) = mx + b$. The number multiplied by $x$ is the slope, or rate of change. The number standing alone is the y-intercept, or starting value.

title: Nonlinear Equations & Functions — Core Skills
summary:
# Functions: The Basics

A function is a machine. You put a number in, it does some arithmetic, and a number comes out. When you see $f(x)$, read it as “f of x.” It does not mean $f$ times $x$.

The one move is substitution. If a question asks for $f(3)$, replace every $x$ in the rule with $3$, then do the arithmetic. Exponents first, then multiply, then add or subtract.

Two things to watch. A negative number squared turns positive, so $(-3)^{2} = 9$. Absolute value bars mean distance from zero, so $|-5| = 5$.

A few extra facts show up again and again: $f(x) + 3$ shifts the graph up $3$ units, the vertex of $(x - h)^{2} + k$ sits at the point $(h, k)$, and a fraction is undefined wherever its bottom equals zero.

title: Quadratic Equations — Core Skills
summary:
# Quadratic Equations: The Basics

A quadratic is an equation where the highest power of $x$ is $2$, like $x^{2} + 7x + 12 = 0$. To factor means to rewrite a sum as a multiplication. A solution, also called a zero or a root, is a value of $x$ that makes the equation true.

The one move is finding two numbers. For $x^{2} + bx + c$, look for two numbers that multiply to $c$ and add to $b$. In $x^{2} + 7x + 12$, the numbers $3$ and $4$ multiply to $12$ and add to $7$, so the factored form is $(x + 3)(x + 4) = 0$.

Then use the zero rule: if two things multiply to zero, one of them must be zero. Set each parenthesis equal to zero and solve. Here $x = -3$ and $x = -4$. Notice how the signs flip.

title: Exponential Functions — Core Skills
summary:
# Exponential Functions: The Basics

Linear growth adds the same amount each step: $10, 20, 30, 40$. Exponential growth multiplies by the same number each step: $10, 20, 40, 80$.

Every exponential function looks like $y = a \cdot b^{x}$. The number $a$ is the starting amount, the value when $x$ is $0$. The base $b$ is the growth factor, the number you multiply by each step. The exponent $x$ is how many steps you take.

The one move is turning a percent into $b$. Growing by 7 percent gives $b = 1 + 0.07 = 1.07$. Shrinking by 7 percent gives $b = 1 - 0.07 = 0.93$. When $b$ is bigger than $1$ the amount grows. When $b$ is between $0$ and $1$ the amount shrinks, which is called decay. The $y$-intercept is always the point $(0, a)$.

title: Polynomials & Factoring — Core Skills
summary:
# Polynomials and Factoring: The Basics

A polynomial is an expression made of terms added or subtracted together, where each term is a number times a power of $x$, like $4x^{3} - 2x^{2} + 7$. The degree is the largest exponent, which is $3$ here. The leading coefficient is the number in front of that term, which is $4$.

To factor means to rewrite something as a multiplication. Always start by pulling out the greatest common factor: the biggest number and the most $x$ letters that every term shares. For $6x^{2} + 15x$, that is $3x$, and the answer is $3x(2x + 5)$.

After the common factor, check for a difference of squares, then use the two-number trick for $x^{2} + bx + c$. Multiply back out to check. A zero comes from a factor: if $f(3) = 0$, then $(x - 3)$ is a factor.

title: Rational Expressions — Core Skills
summary:
# Rational Expressions: The Basics

A rational expression is a fraction with letters in it, like $\frac{3x + 12}{x + 4}$. Two rules run this whole topic.

First, the bottom can never be zero. Any value of $x$ that makes the denominator zero is undefined and gets thrown out. To find it, set the bottom equal to zero and solve.

Second, you may cancel factors, not terms. A factor is something being multiplied. A term is something being added. So factor the top, factor the bottom, then cancel anything that matches. For $\frac{3x + 12}{x + 4}$, the top factors into $3(x + 4)$, the $(x + 4)$ cancels, and the answer is $3$.

You cannot cross out the $x$ letters in $\frac{x + 4}{x + 6}$. Those are terms, not factors, so that fraction is already as simple as it gets.

title: Exponents & Radicals — Core Skills
summary:
# Exponents and Radicals: The Basics

An exponent is the small raised number. It tells you how many times to multiply the base by itself, so $2^{3}$ means $2 \times 2 \times 2 = 8$.

Most SAT questions on this topic come down to four rules. When you multiply powers with the same base, add the exponents. When you divide them, subtract the exponents. When a power is raised to another power, multiply the exponents. And anything raised to the zero power equals $1$.

A square root asks which number times itself gives you the number under the symbol, so $\sqrt{36} = 6$. A negative exponent does not make an answer negative — it means one over that power, so $3^{-2} = \frac{1}{9}$. A fraction exponent is a root: $x^{1/2} = \sqrt{x}$.

Know the rules and the small square roots by sight, and these questions become quick.

title: Geometry Basics — Core Skills
summary:
# Geometry: The Basics

Two words come up over and over. Perimeter is the distance all the way around the outside of a shape, like a fence around a yard. Area is how much flat space is inside, like carpet on a floor.

The formulas are short. Rectangle area is length times width. Square area is side times side. Triangle area is one half times base times height. Perimeter is always just adding up every side.

Angles follow four facts. A straight line is $180°$. A right angle is $90°$. The three angles in any triangle add to $180°$. And when two lines cross, the angles directly across from each other are equal.

For right triangles, use $a^{2} + b^{2} = c^{2}$, where $c$ is the hypotenuse — the long side across from the right angle. The sets 3-4-5, 6-8-10, and 5-12-13 show up constantly.

title: Trigonometry — Core Skills
summary:
# Trigonometry: The Basics

SAT trigonometry starts with one shape: a right triangle, meaning a triangle with one $90°$ angle.

Pick one of the slanted angles and call it theta. Now the three sides get names. The hypotenuse is the longest side, always across from the right angle. The opposite side is across the triangle from theta. The adjacent side is the other leg, the one touching theta.

Three ratios follow, and one word holds all of them: SOH-CAH-TOA. Sine is opposite over hypotenuse. Cosine is adjacent over hypotenuse. Tangent is opposite over adjacent.

So the whole move is: label the three sides for your angle, then pick the ratio the question asks for.

A few values are worth memorizing, especially $\sin 30° = \frac{1}{2}$ and $\tan 45° = 1$. And one identity is always true: $\sin^{2}\theta + \cos^{2}\theta = 1$.

title: Circles — Core Skills
summary:
# Circles: The Basics

Two words do most of the work here. The radius is the distance from the center of a circle out to the edge. The diameter is the distance all the way across, through the center. The diameter is twice the radius, so if you know one you know the other.

Then there are two formulas. Area, the space inside, is $\pi r^{2}$. Circumference, the distance around the edge, is $2\pi r$. Both use the radius, never the diameter. When a question gives you a diameter, cut it in half first — that one habit prevents most circle mistakes.

On a grid, a circle is written $(x - h)^{2} + (y - k)^{2} = r^{2}$. The center is $(h, k)$, and the signs flip when you read them. The number on the right is the radius squared, so take its square root to get the radius.

title: Statistics & Data Interpretation — Core Skills
summary:
# Statistics & Data Interpretation: The Basics

A data set is a list of numbers, and the SAT asks the same three questions about it over and over.

The **mean** is the average. Add every number in the list, then divide by how many numbers there are. For 4, 8, 6, 10, and 2, the total is 30, and 30 divided by 5 is 6.

The **median** is the middle number after you put the list in order from smallest to largest. Sorting first is the step people skip, so write the sorted list down. If the list has an even number of values, add the two middle numbers and divide by 2.

The **range** is the biggest number minus the smallest number. For 2, 4, 6, 8, 10 the range is 10 minus 2, which is 8.

Mean and median describe the center of a list. Range describes how spread out it is.

title: Data & Statistics — Core Skills
summary:
# Data & Statistics: The Basics

A two-way table sorts a group of people two ways at once, like boys and girls across Yes and No. Each box inside the table is a cell, and it holds a count of people.

The Total column on the right is the row added across. The Total row along the bottom is the column added down. The bottom-right corner is everyone.

Most questions ask you to turn a count into a fraction or a percent. The count you want goes on top. The group the question asks about goes on the bottom. If it says "of all 50 students," the bottom is 50. If it says "of the boys," the bottom is only the boys.

To make a percent, turn the bottom number into 100 if you can, or divide the top by the bottom and move the decimal point two places to the right.

title: Scatterplots & Line of Best Fit — Core Skills
summary:
# Scatterplots & Line of Best Fit: The Basics

A scatterplot is a graph made of dots. Each dot is one thing that got measured twice, like a student's study hours and that same student's test score.

A line of best fit is a straight line drawn through the middle of the dots to show their general direction.

Read the dots from left to right. Rising dots mean a positive association: as x goes up, y goes up. Falling dots mean a negative association: as x goes up, y goes down.

The line comes with an equation like y = 2x + 5. The number in front of x is the slope, and it says how much y changes each time x goes up by 1. The number added at the end is the y-intercept, the predicted y when x is 0.

To predict, put the number in for x, multiply, then add.

title: Probability & Two-Way Tables — Core Skills
summary:
# Probability & Two-Way Tables: The Basics

Probability is a number that says how likely something is, and it is always written as a fraction built the same way: the number of outcomes you want on top, the total number of outcomes on the bottom.

In a bag with 3 red, 5 blue, and 2 green marbles, the total is 10, so the probability of drawing red is 3 over 10.

If the question uses the word not, count everything that does not match and put that count on top. Not red would be 7 out of 10.

The part to read carefully is the beginning of the question, because it names your group. "A student is picked at random" means the group is everyone. "A junior is picked" means the group is only the juniors, so the junior total goes on the bottom.

Reduce your fraction at the end. Every probability lands between 0 and 1.
